paragraphs: This paper studies fast least-squares regression with a stronger requirement than obtaining a good overall fit: every coordinate of the computed solution must stay close to the corresponding coordinate of the optimal solution. The permitted error depends on the optimal residual, the matrix pseudoinverse norm, the number of coordinates, and an accuracy parameter.

The usual sketching strategy compresses the regression problem using a random matrix before solving it. The authors show that obtaining their coordinate-wise guarantee requires dense sketching matrices. They also establish a suitable distribution of dense sketches using ε⁻²d log³(n/δ) rows, with success probability at least 1−δ. Despite their density, these sketches permit computing the compressed matrix in O(nd log n) time.

The required row count is nearly optimal up to logarithmic factors and improves the earlier bound described in the abstract. A framework based on Oblivious Coordinate-wise Embedding makes the analysis simpler and more general, and extends the result to dense sketches for fast tensor products of vectors.
icml-2023-a-nearly-optimal-bound-for-fas.tldr: Dense but efficiently computable sketches enable nearly optimal compression for regression with coordinate-wise error guarantees.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning system can perform differently when its observations or internal policy components change. This matters when moving between simulated and real environments, where conditions do not match perfectly. The paper develops an adversarial learning framework for distributional reinforcement learning that helps diagnose which parts of a system contribute to performance loss.

The central tool is an influence measure adapted from statistics. It is constructed using information geometry and has invariance properties. The framework considers influences arising both outside the policy, through state observations, and inside it, through policy structure. This provides a shared way to examine sources of sensitivity that might otherwise be analyzed separately.

The authors demonstrate three diagnostic uses: locating fragile states along trajectories, assessing instability associated with policy architecture, and identifying unusually sensitive policy parameters. These findings concern understanding vulnerability within a learned system. They make the framework useful for identifying where performance is sensitive, without establishing that the resulting diagnoses alone solve the broader challenge of deployment outside simulation.
icml-2023-adversarial-learning-of-distri.tldr: An information-geometric influence measure diagnoses sensitivity in distributional reinforcement learning observations, architectures, and policy parameters.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines labeled and unlabeled examples, but the labeled examples may not represent all classes equally. If one class is more likely to receive labels than another, the presence of a label itself carries information. The paper studies this missing-not-at-random setting, where ignoring the labeling process can bias learning.

The proposed approach first estimates the mechanism that determines which examples receive labels. It then uses inverse propensity weighting to compensate for unequal labeling probabilities. The correction is presented as applicable to any semi-supervised learning algorithm, including methods that use data augmentation. This makes the labeling mechanism an explicit part of the learning procedure.

The authors also introduce a likelihood ratio test for assessing whether label availability is informative. Together, the test and correction address both recognizing the problem and responding to it. Evaluations cover several datasets, including two medical datasets with constructed, pseudo-realistic missing-data scenarios. Those scenarios examine the methods under deliberately modeled labeling patterns rather than establishing performance for every naturally occurring medical labeling process.
icml-2023-are-labels-informative-in-semi.tldr: Estimating how labels go missing enables a weighting correction for class-dependent labeling bias in semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Transforming one structured object into another can require a sequence of symbolic tree operations. Learning such sequences is difficult because discrete operations do not directly support gradient-based training. This paper introduces a differentiable tree interpreter that translates high-level symbolic operations into matrix operations on tensors, making those operations usable within an end-to-end learning system.

The resulting Differentiable Tree Machine combines the interpreter with external memory and an agent that selects operations sequentially. Its architecture connects a learned decision process to explicit tree manipulation. That connection matters for compositional generalization: the system is tested on whether learned operations can be combined successfully in structures outside the training distribution.

On the reported synthetic semantic parsing and language generation tasks, the machine reaches 100% out-of-distribution compositional generalization, while the listed Transformer and recurrent tree or sequence baselines remain below 30%. The authors also describe the model as highly interpretable. These results establish a striking advantage on the studied synthetic transformations, with the explicit operation sequence providing a readable account of its computation.
icml-2023-differentiable-tree-operations.tldr: A differentiable tree interpreter enables an interpretable model to achieve perfect compositional generalization on the studied synthetic tasks.

paragraphs: An instruction-following agent must connect words to what it observes and what it can do. Establishing those connections often requires specialized engineering or substantial human interaction data. This paper investigates using a pretrained vision-language model as a source of supervision, transferring its existing language grounding into an embodied agent's task environment.

The method combines model distillation with hindsight experience replay. After an agent acts, the vision-language model generates language describing that behavior. These retrospective descriptions become supervision for learning connections between language and action. Prompting controls which aspects of the behavior the descriptions emphasize, allowing the same source model to teach different task-relevant meanings.

In a rendered 3D environment, the authors teach interactions with novel objects using object names or features such as color. With a few prompting examples, they also teach familiar abstract categories and newly specified categories based on arbitrary preferences. The findings show how broad visual-language knowledge can be repurposed into more specific embodied groundings through supervision generated from the agent's own behavior.
icml-2023-distilling-internet-scale-visi.tldr: A pretrained vision-language model teaches embodied agents language grounding by retrospectively describing their behavior.

paragraphs: Multiview self-supervised learning often encourages representations to remain unchanged when an input is transformed. This invariance can remove information about the transformation itself. That loss becomes a problem for downstream tasks that need to know how an input changed, even when its semantic content remains similar.

DUET addresses this by organizing representations as two-dimensional matrices and retaining transformation-related information through approximate equivariance. The intended representation remains semantically expressive while also reflecting changes applied to the input. Its structured organization is central to the proposal: the paper compares it with representations that are invariant and unstructured, as well as ones that are equivariant but unstructured.

The authors report controlled generation with lower reconstruction error than SimCLR and ESSL, and state that those comparison methods do not support controllability in the studied setting. DUET also improves accuracy on several discriminative tasks and improves transfer learning. Together, these results support retaining organized transformation information when a representation must serve both recognition and controllable generation.
icml-2023-duet-2d-structured-and-approxi.tldr: DUET organizes representations to preserve transformation information, improving controlled generation and several recognition and transfer tasks.

paragraphs: Hawkes processes model event sequences in which earlier events influence the occurrence of later ones. The influence is described by a kernel. Exponential kernels are data efficient but poorly suited to estimating delayed responses, while nonparametric kernels can require large datasets. FaDIn targets a more flexible parametric alternative for applications where timing delays matter.

The method fits general parametric kernels with finite support using a fast gradient-based solver for an ℓ₂ objective. It operates on a discretized representation of event times, and the paper provides theoretical support for that discretization. This connects the computational simplification to the inference problem rather than relying solely on its practical speed.

Numerical experiments demonstrate statistical and computational efficiency. The authors also apply the method to stimulus-related patterns in magnetoencephalography brain recordings. In that application, the flexibility of the parametric kernels produces better estimates of pattern latency than the state of the art described in the abstract. The result highlights the value of modeling delayed event influence explicitly.
icml-2023-fadin-fast-discretized-inferen.tldr: FaDIn efficiently fits flexible Hawkes-process kernels and improves latency estimation for stimulus-related brain-signal patterns.

paragraphs: Feedback for a physical skill needs to explain how a learner should change their behavior. A simple correct-or-incorrect signal may not provide that guidance, while hand-written feedback templates can be difficult to transfer to new domains. CORGI is designed to generate natural-language corrections from examples of student and expert behavior.

The model receives a pair of trajectories: one showing the student's actions and one showing expert performance. It uses this comparison to produce a correction intended to help the student improve. The authors collect training data across drawing, steering, and joint movement, addressing varied forms of physical control within the same modeling approach.

Automatic and human evaluations support three findings. CORGI produces valid feedback for previously unseen student trajectories, outperforms baselines in domains with new control dynamics, and improves student learning in an interactive drawing task. These results connect feedback generation to an observed learning benefit in drawing, while the other evaluations examine whether useful corrections transfer across behaviors and control settings.
icml-2023-generating-language-correction.tldr: CORGI compares student and expert trajectories to generate language corrections, with demonstrated learning benefits in an interactive drawing task.

paragraphs: Decision support can fail when experts must decide for themselves whether to trust each automated recommendation. This paper changes the interaction: the system supplies a set of candidate labels, and the expert must choose from that set. The expert therefore solves a restricted classification problem instead of judging whether to accept a single machine prediction.

Conformal prediction controls the trade-off between set size and the probability of excluding the true label. Smaller sets simplify the expert's task but can remove the correct answer; larger sets preserve more choices while leaving a harder decision. The authors develop an efficient, near-optimal search procedure to find the conformal predictor under which experts benefit most.

Simulations using both synthetic predictions and real expert predictions indicate that the system may improve expert accuracy. They also show robustness to the accuracy of the underlying classifier. The evidence supports this constrained-choice design as a potentially useful form of assistance, while preserving the central trade-off: excluding the true label directly prevents an expert from selecting it.
icml-2023-improving-expert-predictions-w.tldr: Conformal prediction sets can improve expert decisions by restricting choices while balancing task difficulty against exclusion of the correct label.

paragraphs: Kernel QuantTree detects changes in multivariate data by monitoring a histogram. Its bins come from a nonlinear partition of the input space, designed to match specified target probabilities. The partition also encourages compact bins that follow the data distribution, making the histogram responsive to changes in how observations are distributed.

The paper proves that statistics defined over this histogram do not depend on the particular stationary data distribution. This allows detection thresholds to be chosen in advance to control false positives. The kernel construction also makes monitoring invariant to rotations and translations of the input, so changing the coordinate orientation or position does not change the monitoring behavior.

These properties matter because a detector must distinguish real distribution changes from artifacts of its representation and threshold choice. The authors state that KQT needs no preprocessing such as PCA. Experiments show stronger detection power than the compared nonparametric state-of-the-art methods, together with reliable false-positive control. The contribution combines a distribution-independent thresholding result with an empirically effective nonlinear partition.
icml-2023-kernel-quanttree-5fa41f54e7.tldr: Kernel QuantTree uses nonlinear histogram bins to detect distribution changes with theoretically controlled thresholds and rotation-and-translation invariance.

paragraphs: Causal disentanglement aims to recover hidden variables, their causal relationships, and how they produce observed data. This paper studies a specific linear setting: the hidden causal model is linear, and the observations are a linear transformation of its variables. Identifiability asks whether those underlying components can be uniquely determined.

The authors establish complementary results about interventions. If even one latent variable lacks an intervention, distinct models can exist that the data cannot distinguish. Conversely, one intervention on each latent variable is sufficient for identifiability in the studied setting. The first statement describes a failure of general identification, rather than claiming that every individual case with a missing intervention is ambiguous.

The proof generalizes matrix RQ decomposition using conditions determined by the causal model's partial ordering. The authors also develop a disentanglement method that accurately recovers latent causal models on synthetic and semi-synthetic data, and illustrate its use with single-cell RNA sequencing measurements. The practical results accompany a precise account of when intervention coverage supports recovery.
icml-2023-linear-causal-disentanglement-.tldr: For linear latent causal models observed through linear mixtures, one intervention per latent variable is sufficient for identifiability.

paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition involves training data with uneven class frequencies. Contrastive learning can struggle in this setting, and combining it with logit adjustment has often lacked a unified theoretical explanation. This paper seeks both to explain that combination and to derive a stronger learning objective from the explanation.

The authors identify a mismatch in what standard contrastive learning tries to preserve. Maximizing mutual information between latent features and input data does not explicitly account for ground-truth labels, and therefore does not address class imbalance through that objective. They instead formulate recognition around maximizing mutual information between features and labels, placing class identity directly into the information being retained.

This formulation produces a loss that integrates contrastive learning and logit adjustment within one theoretical approach. The resulting method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the reported long-tailed recognition benchmarks. It also works effectively for image segmentation, extending the empirical evidence beyond image classification. The main contribution is a principled connection between the information objective and the imbalance correction.
icml-2023-long-tailed-recognition-by-mut.tldr: Maximizing information between features and labels yields a unified contrastive-learning and logit-adjustment loss for long-tailed recognition.

paragraphs: Streaming speech recognition faces a timing trade-off. Using only current and past audio allows quick outputs, while waiting for future audio can improve recognition accuracy. A fixed future-context window imposes waiting even when additional context may not be equally useful throughout an utterance.

The Adaptive Non-Causal Attention Transducer makes that choice dynamically. It decides when to use future frames and how much future context to access at different points in the audio stream. Although the architecture is non-causal because it can consult future input, it is designed to operate in a streaming, low-latency manner. New regularization algorithms work with this adaptive mechanism.

Experiments on public and production-scale voice-assistant datasets compare both accuracy and latency. The authors report accuracy comparable to non-causal configurations while substantially reducing latency and bringing it closer to causal systems. The result supports selective lookahead as a way to improve the trade-off, without claiming that future context becomes free or that latency always matches a strictly causal model.
icml-2023-lookahead-when-it-matters-adap.tldr: ANCAT dynamically selects future audio context to retain non-causal recognition accuracy while reducing streaming latency.

paragraphs: Loss-Guided Diffusion aims to steer a pretrained diffusion model using a differentiable loss, without additional training. The loss expresses a desired property of the output, allowing generation to be controlled through the sampling process. The framework is designed to integrate with diffusion models and work with various efficient samplers.

The difficulty is computing the guidance signal: its exact form involves an intractable integral. Existing approaches approximate that signal using a single point estimate, and the authors show that this introduces substantial approximation errors. Their alternative uses Monte Carlo sampling, drawing multiple samples from a suitable distribution to reduce the bias of the guidance estimate.

The method is effective in synthetic and real-world settings spanning image super-resolution, text- or label-conditioned image generation, and motion synthesis. In particular, it guides a pretrained motion model to follow specified paths and avoid obstacles that challenged prior methods. These findings connect a better approximation of the guidance term to more effective control across several generation tasks.
icml-2023-loss-guided-diffusion-models-f.tldr: Monte Carlo guidance reduces approximation bias when controlling pretrained diffusion models with differentiable losses and no additional training.

paragraphs: In predict-then-optimize systems, a model's predictions become inputs to a downstream optimization problem. For example, predicted coefficients can determine the objective of a linear program. The learning problem therefore concerns the decisions produced by predictions, making the relationship between training loss and optimization behavior central.

Maximum optimality margin constructs the learning loss from the downstream problem's optimality conditions. Its max-margin formulation is designed to provide computational efficiency and favorable theoretical learning properties. The approach addresses difficulties identified in earlier methods, including intractable optimization, weaker generalization bounds, and reliance on strong conditions such as loss calibration or an absence of constraints.

A particularly useful feature is that training requires observations of optimal solutions rather than the objective functions that produced them. This connects contextual prediction with inverse linear programming, where observed decisions inform the underlying optimization model. The authors analyze both contextual and context-free versions, study offline and online learning settings, and demonstrate the method through numerical experiments. The shared optimality-based loss provides the unifying mechanism.
icml-2023-maximum-optimality-margin-a-un.tldr: Maximum optimality margin learns from observed optimal decisions using a loss derived from downstream linear-program optimality conditions.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning concerns adapting to a new task with limited examples, but meta-learning methods can still require many training tasks. MetaModulation addresses the separate problem of having too few tasks available during meta-training. Its strategy is to make the available task experience denser and more varied through learned changes inside the network.

A modulation network adjusts batch-normalization parameters during meta-training. Applying adjustments at multiple network levels increases task diversity beyond what a single-layer modification provides. The variational version treats modulation parameters as latent variables, explicitly representing uncertainty associated with the limited task collection. Extending this modulation across all layers produces variational feature hierarchies.

Ablation studies support using learnable modulation at different levels and show benefits from the probabilistic variants. Across four few-task meta-learning benchmarks, MetaModulation and its variational versions consistently outperform the state-of-the-art alternatives considered. The findings support feature modulation as a way to improve learning under task scarcity, with hierarchical variation and uncertainty modeling both contributing to the approach.
icml-2023-metamodulation-learning-variat.tldr: MetaModulation improves learning from few training tasks by varying features across network layers and modeling modulation uncertainty.

paragraphs: Training large neural networks requires managing many tensors within limited device memory. Existing approaches can reduce memory demand through techniques such as spilling, recomputation, reduced precision, or pruning, but may add training time, affect accuracy, or require substantial manual changes. MODeL focuses on optimizing tensor lifetimes and memory locations automatically.

The method formulates these decisions jointly as an integer linear program. Treating them together allows the optimization to consider how tensor storage requirements interact during training. The authors introduce simplifications to the mathematical encoding so that an off-the-shelf solver can handle problems at the scale of state-of-the-art neural networks.

Experiments show that MODeL takes only seconds to enable training with 30% less memory on average. The authors report these savings without the drawbacks they identify in the alternative techniques. The stated reduction is an experimental average, rather than a guaranteed saving for each network. The contribution is a tractable joint optimization of memory use that can be applied to existing models automatically.
icml-2023-model-memory-optimizations-for.tldr: MODeL jointly optimizes tensor lifetimes and storage locations, enabling training with 30% less memory on average in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Higher-order correlation clustering offers an expressive way to formulate clustering problems, and local search heuristics have been developed for several applications. Yet obtaining a candidate clustering and certifying its optimality are different challenges. The paper starts from the difficulty of certification, which is NP-hard and complicated in practice by the size and complexity of the problem formulation.

The authors investigate partial optimality for a restricted setting: complete graphs with cubic objective functions. The goal is to establish conditions that certify parts of an optimal solution, rather than requiring a certificate for the entire clustering. This shifts attention toward conclusions that may be available even when full optimality is difficult to establish.

The work includes algorithms for checking the proposed conditions and implementations of those algorithms. Numerical studies on two datasets examine their effect. The contribution therefore combines mathematical conditions with a practical route for testing them. Its stated scope remains the complete-graph, cubic-objective case; the abstract does not claim a general solver for all higher-order correlation clustering problems.
icml-2023-partial-optimality-in-cubic-co.tldr: The paper develops testable partial-optimality conditions for correlation clustering on complete graphs with cubic objectives.

paragraphs: Sampling methods were once prominent in combinatorial optimization, but older approaches could be inefficient and require problem-specific design. More recent learned solvers reduce dependence on hand-crafted heuristics, yet may depend on matching their training distribution and struggle with large instances. This paper revisits sampling in light of newer computational techniques.

The approach draws on advances in gradient-based discrete Markov chain Monte Carlo and parallel exploration of neighboring solutions on accelerators. These methods use information about the optimization landscape to guide search. The authors find that modern sampling can provide general-purpose solvers that require no training while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art combinatorial optimization methods.

Experiments cover vertex-cover selection, graph partitioning, and routing. They show better speed-quality trade-offs than the learning-based approaches considered, and sometimes better performance than commercial solvers or specialized algorithms. The qualified comparison matters: the finding is competitive performance across the studied tasks, with occasional wins over stronger solver categories, rather than universal superiority. It makes sampling a credible option for training-free optimization.
icml-2023-revisiting-sampling-for-combin.tldr: Modern discrete sampling and parallel search provide training-free combinatorial solvers with competitive speed-quality trade-offs.

paragraphs: Many convex optimization algorithms repeatedly use projections whose defining matrices change over time. Recomputing the relevant quantities can be expensive. This paper extends projection-maintenance data structures to matrices built with Kronecker products, targeting a structured setting in which the projection must stay useful through a sequence of updates.

The setup combines a constraint matrix with a positive semidefinite weight matrix that has a sparse eigenbasis. Two Kronecker constructions are considered, using either the weight matrix and an identity matrix or two copies of its square root. At each iteration, the weight matrix undergoes a low-rank change and a new query vector arrives. The data structure must approximately apply the current projection to that vector.

The authors design a fast dynamic structure with approximation guarantees and robustness against an adaptive adversary. They also use differential privacy tools to reduce the randomness the structure needs, improving running time further. Here, privacy techniques serve an algorithmic role in efficient, adaptive computation within the stated matrix-structure assumptions.
icml-2023-sketching-meets-differential-p.tldr: A dynamic data structure maintains Kronecker-structured projections efficiently, using differential privacy tools to reduce randomness and resist adaptive adversaries.

paragraphs: Multi-channel images have structured relationships across their dimensions, but their size makes statistical prediction challenging. This paper studies scalar-on-tensor regression, where a multidimensional image is used to predict a single response. Motivated by solar flare forecasting, it extends a Tensor Gaussian Process model with an integrated dimensionality-reduction step.

The method first estimates a smaller latent tensor for each observed tensor through tensor contraction. A multilinear Tensor Gaussian Process then uses these reduced representations for prediction. During contraction, anisotropic total-variation regularization encourages the latent tensors to be both sparse and smooth. This makes the reduction sensitive to structure rather than treating dimensionality alone as the concern.

The authors propose an alternating proximal gradient descent algorithm to estimate the model. They validate the approach through extensive simulations and an application to solar flare forecasting with multi-channel images. The work links structured compression and probabilistic regression in one approach, so the large imaging input is represented in a smaller tensor form before prediction while retaining an explicit tensor-based modeling framework.
icml-2023-tensor-gaussian-process-with-c.tldr: Tensor contraction creates sparse, smooth reduced image representations for Tensor Gaussian Process regression and solar flare forecasting.

paragraphs: A segmentation can overlap the target image well while still getting its structural organization wrong. Topology-aware objectives address that problem, but global topological summaries can overlook where individual features occur. This paper focuses on preserving topological features in their correct spatial locations, not merely obtaining the right overall topological counts.

The authors introduce induced matchings from persistent homology to match persistence barcodes in a spatially appropriate way. From these matches, they define the Betti matching error, an interpretable metric that evaluates topology at the level of individual features. It addresses limitations of Betti number error, which does not provide the same feature-wise assessment.

The new error is differentiable and efficient enough to serve directly as a training loss. Across six datasets, using it significantly improves segmentation networks' topological performance while maintaining performance on traditional scores. This means the reported structural improvements do not come at the expense of those conventional measurements. The contribution connects a more spatially faithful evaluation metric with an objective that can guide learning.
icml-2023-topologically-faithful-image-s.tldr: Betti matching provides a differentiable segmentation loss that preserves spatially corresponding topological features and improves structural accuracy.

paragraphs: Incremental learning trains a model on tasks as they arrive, while trying to retain performance on earlier tasks. For node-level graph prediction, the challenge includes dependencies between examples and changes in graph structure. New tasks can alter the context in which previously learned nodes are represented, complicating the preservation of earlier knowledge.

The paper formalizes and analyzes inductive node-wise graph incremental learning with this structural evolution. It shows that structural shifts can change the input distribution of existing tasks and thereby increase the risk of catastrophic forgetting. This identifies an additional source of forgetting tied to the changing graph itself.

The proposed Structural-Shift-Risk-Mitigation method uses regularization to reduce the effect of these changes. Empirical studies on several benchmark datasets show that it can be adapted to improve state-of-the-art graph neural network incremental-learning frameworks in the inductive setting. The result supports treating graph evolution as an explicit learning risk, with a flexible correction that works alongside existing incremental-learning methods.
icml-2023-towards-robust-graph-increment.tldr: SSRM reduces forgetting in inductive graph incremental learning by regularizing against risks introduced by evolving graph structure.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo estimators approximate integrals using samples, and control variates can reduce the variability of those estimates. Building effective control variates can itself require many samples, which becomes costly when sampling or function evaluation is expensive. The burden grows when several related integrals must be computed, either together or in sequence.

This paper introduces vector-valued control variates that reduce the variance of multiple estimators jointly. The key benefit is information transfer between integration tasks, reducing the need to gather a large sample collection separately for each one. The construction focuses on kernel interpolants and develops a generalized Stein identity together with matrix-valued Stein reproducing kernels.

The authors demonstrate the method on multifidelity modeling, Bayesian inference for dynamical systems, and model evidence calculation through thermodynamic integration. These applications illustrate the intended setting: multiple integrals whose relationship can be used during estimation. The contribution turns variance reduction into a shared problem across related tasks, providing a mathematical construction for using that relationship rather than treating each estimate in isolation.
icml-2023-vector-valued-control-variates.tldr: Vector-valued control variates share information across related integrals to jointly reduce Monte Carlo variance and sampling needs.

paragraphs: Learning representations jointly across knowledge graphs depends on aligning entities that correspond across sources. Embedding-based alignment methods have made progress, but their underlying behavior is not always clear. This paper explains two model families, translation-based and aggregation-based methods, through the perspective of the conventional similarity flooding algorithm.

The central theoretical result is that embedding learning in these models seeks a fixed point of pairwise entity similarities. A fixed point is a stable configuration under the relevant update process. This interpretation connects learned embeddings with an established similarity-computation procedure, providing a common account of how the studied models arrive at their alignment-related representations.

The authors provide experimental evidence supporting that analysis and introduce two simple methods inspired by fixed-point computation in similarity flooding. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate their effectiveness. The work therefore uses the explanation constructively: the connection helps interpret existing models and motivates new methods. Its scope is the analyzed translation-based and aggregation-based alignment models, rather than a claim about every possible knowledge-graph embedding approach.
icml-2023-what-makes-entities-similar-a-.tldr: A fixed-point interpretation connects embedding-based entity alignment to similarity flooding and motivates two effective alignment methods.
